each with the perforated dinner-table conversation card printed as the tear-off strip at the bottom; the ten questions live in the §03b printing spec), 60 artifact cards (the numbered Gauntlet deck built on the instructor laptop in the week-before window), 39 mission/claim/verdict cards (12 mission, 15 claim, 12 verdict, counted against the Day 2 and Day 3 materials lists), 12 verdict-report templates (Day 3, one per camper, counted against the Day 3 materials list), 12 claim-confidence sheets (Day 3, one per camper, counted against the Day 3 materials list), 12 Day 1 answer cards, 12 producer checklists (laminated in Hour 2, packed in the Day 1 box), 36 blunder sheets (3 binders x 12, this spring's blunders, selected and laid out on the instructor laptop in the week-before window, see Phase 6), 12 question-craft sheets, 12 transcription cards, 12 wiring-diagram cards, 6 queue slips, 6 blank claim tags, 12 debug log sheets, 12 failure log sheets (Day 5), 12 before-and-after portfolio pages (Day 5), 12 overnight log charts (Day 4), 2 ship lists (one posted, one spare), plus the Day 2 grading sheet ("AI vs. you") for the grading station, 12 deploy log sheets and 12 graph charts (Day 4), 12 tally sheets (Day 2 only), 12 panel scorecards (Day 8), 12 QC-gate page templates (Day 8), 12 credit-roll templates (Day 9), 12 diplomas (Day 10), 12 taste-panel award cards (Day 10), the showcase program master (one page, filled in Thursday from the ship list; Friday's parent copies print from it), and 24 gallery labels (Day 10), the one-page paper attendance sheet and the one-page paper med/incident log sheet (the tech-outage paper backstop, filed in the instructor folder at Hour 4), 12 blank incident report forms, one page each (the field list lives in the Incident handling bullet's same-hour rule below; the forms file into the instructor folder at Hour 4, and the folder rides in the instructor's field bag on field missions, so a Tier 2 or Tier 3 on a walk has the form in hand), the two one-page hospital handoff sheets (the nearest emergency department's name, address, and phone, mapped at the T-2 site visit, print on both; one blank rides with the paramedics when a Tier 3 transports, the other stays in the folder as the blank spare; both file into the instructor folder at Hour 4 beside the med/allergy sheet), 10 one-page end-of-day summary digest templates (one per teaching day, the field list the pickup-row names; each day's filled page stays in the instructor folder as the session's daily record), the ten one-page handout answer keys plus the one-page Gauntlet answer key (one page each, filed in the instructor folder at Hour 4), and the two one-page lightning abort cards (laminated at Hour 2 with the other cards: one lives in the field bag's front pocket, one spare files in the instructor folder at Hour 4; the Hour 4 re-stage trashes the prior session's laminated pair before these file, so the pocket and the folder hold this session's cards only), the four briefing pages (two copies of the shop-owner briefing sheet, the Day 6 guest brief, the Day 8 judge brief), and the one-page founder's own checklist (the fresh checklist the next session opens: filed in the instructor folder at Hour 4, retired to the trip folder at move-out), plus the one-page crew-rotation board (Days 1-10, three name-role pairs per day in alphabetical roster order, printed inside the run's margin), plus the one-page buddy-pair board (six first-name pairs in alphabetical roster order, printed inside the run's margin), and the allergy action plans for every camper with a food allergy or EpiPen authorization on file (one page each, printed from the parent-provided PDFs collected with the Typeform intake, inside the run's margin), and 10 morning checklists (one per teaching day: the 8:45 deferred-transcription read-off the joint beat reads aloud, plus the ruled margin lines the pickup row's log beats write into all day; laid out in the week-before window, see Phase 6; packed one per day-box at Hour 2), plus 10 day-box lid prep checklists (one per day: the day's 30-minute prep checklist Hour 2 tapes inside the box lid, exported one page per day from this page's day-prep sections in the week-before window, see Phase 6). Then open the phone's Settings and confirm automatic date-and-time is toggled on: the close-of-day re-verification reads this phone's automatic date, so the toggle is the authority's on-switch; if it is off, turn it on and leave it on all session, and if the phone sat on a manual date after travel, let one network-synced date read land before relying on it. Clip the instructor medical card face-down beside the instructor phone on the instructor table, so the room incapacitation script's clip line has its staged artifact; it rides in the field bag's zip phone pocket on field missions, per the safety plan's field-mission morning motion. Initial the check on the Session Zero checklist beside the test-text confirmation. If the instructor phone is replaced or factory-reset mid-session, the new or reset phone gets the toggle check before its first close-of-day re-verification: open the phone's Settings, confirm automatic date-and-time is toggled on, turn it on and leave it on all session if it is off, let one network-synced date read land, and initial the re-check in the morning checklist margin; the close-of-day re-verification never reads a new or reset phone's date until the re-check is initialed, so a replaced or wiped device cannot hand the re-verification an unverified date. If the replacement phone cannot reach a network before its first close-of-day re-verification, because its line is not activated and it has no data and no venue Wi-Fi, the re-check does not stall the close: on a named no-data branch the instructor logs 'replacement phone has no network, re-check not completed, date unverified ' with the date in the morning checklist margin, and the close-of-day re-verification runs the dead-phone close fallback on this live phone, the margin-line read alone with a 'phone has no network, date not cross-checked' margin log and a reach-a-network-before-next-prep clause, so the unverified date is still never read. The re-check gives the network-synced date read a fixed wait budget of five minutes of wall time at the close, timed on the room clock, and inside the budget it pins an attempt sequence of three named attempts, so no passive wait can burn the budget on one stalled attempt: attempt one is the initial read with automatic date-and-time already confirmed on, watching the read for the first two minutes; attempt two fires at the start of the third minute, an airplane-mode cycle, airplane mode on for thirty seconds then off, then a fresh read; attempt three is the venue network join, venue Wi-Fi or the founder's hotspot, then one final read before the budget ends; and if the fifth minute ends with no synced read the no-data branch fires at once and the re-verification proceeds with the margin-line read alone, so a stalled sync can never hold the close past five minutes. Every attempt also leaves an attempt log in the morning checklist margin beside the re-check: after each attempt the instructor writes the attempt number, the room-clock time, and initials, so a failed attempt always leaves a paper trace, and each failed attempt's line also carries one failure word, its failure signature: stale when the phone displayed an old unmoved date, spinning when the sync indicator ran without resolving, blank when no date display appeared at all, so the margin records why the sync failed and not just that it did; when the margin's words disagree, stale on one attempt and spinning on another, the mixed-margin rule names which word outranks the others: the latest attempt's word outranks the earlier ones, because it reflects the phone's most recent state, so the morning retry chases the latest attempt's fix first and only falls back to the earlier words if the latest fix lands and the read still fails; the fallback-chain cap ends the chase at two morning retries: the first morning's retry runs the latest attempt's fix, the second morning's retry runs the fallback fix from the earlier words, and if the second morning's retry still fails after its fix lands, the instructor stops chasing the margin's words and takes the dead-phone close fallback, the margin-line read alone with the margin log standing, at that close and every later close, instead of a third morning retry; only a genuinely new network, an activated line, venue Wi-Fi, or a founder hotspot not available on any earlier attempt, restarts the chase as a new first attempt. When the cap fires, the instructor writes the cap log line in the morning checklist margin beside that close's margin log and initials it beside the words: 'chain capped after second morning retry, fallback read used, date not cross-checked ', so the capped stop carries the same attribution as the successful-read log, whose read log carries the attempt number, the synced date, the room-clock time, and initials. The ordinary no-network close keeps the standing margin log 'phone has no network, date not cross-checked', so the margin shows a capped chain and an ordinary no-network close as two different lines. The date slot on the cap log line always carries the close's calendar date, never the phone's displayed date, so the paper trail never reads the unverified phone date, the one the line says was not cross-checked, as a fact. The date slot takes the spelled-out month and day, written 'October 2', never digits like '10/2', so the paper trail never reads an ambiguous date as a fact. A successful read logs the attempt number, the synced date, the room-clock time, and initials, and the margin ends up showing the full sequence of attempts the close actually ran. The synced-date slot on the successful-read log takes the spelled-out month and day, written 'October 2', never digits like '10/2', so the paper trail never reads an ambiguous date as a fact. The no-data branch fires when the budget ends without a synced read, never on the phone's signal display, so a phone showing bars with no data takes the same branch. At the next morning's 8:45 prep the instructor reads the failure words before the retry, because a run of spinning lines points the retry at the network while a run of stale lines points it at the phone's date storage, then retries the toggle check on the replacement phone when a network is available, an activated line, venue Wi-Fi, or a hotspot from the founder's cell; if the phone still has no network the branch re-fires at that close and the margin log stands for a second consecutive day. Label the table-supply caddy 'TABLE SUPPLY' with one of the 4 markers from the equipment shelf (the 8:45 morning prep, the §07 shop-tools row, and the §08 move-out pack list all pull the caddy by name as the 'labeled table-supply caddy', so the label is set here at Hour 4 before anything consumes it), then stage the 12 blunt-tip table scissors in the labeled table-supply caddy on the equipment shelf, bought once as reusable shop stock inside the $931 shop-tools startup line, about $8 for the caddy (the scissors bought the same way, and the fidget tools and earplugs riding the same caddy); the caddy rides out with the morning room setup and returns to the shelf at teardown, which is what the safety plan's 'sit at the tables freely' line describes during lessons. Stage the fidget tools and the noise-reducing earplugs in the same caddy at the same time, bought once as reusable shop stock inside the $931 shop-tools startup line, so the accommodations bullet's sensory supports ride the morning pull the caddy already makes. Coil the 6-foot HDMI cable and the USB-C-to-HDMI adapter on the equipment shelf, plug the instructor laptop into the venue's room screen through both, and confirm the fail-of-the-day slide fills the screen (the adapter covers the instructor's USB-C-only laptop; the venue cable is never assumed); the cable and adapter live on the shelf all session and are pulled in Day 1 and Day 6 prep. Set the flatbed document scanner on the door table (it stays there all session, never in a day-box); plug it into the instructor laptop; create the twelve per-camper gallery folders on the instructor laptop, one per camper off the Airtable roster, and run one test scan into one of them so the scan lands in a folder that exists; create the session gallery folder on the instructor laptop beside the twelve per-camper gallery folders, and leave the lid closed. Put three fresh scan-tab sticky-note pads (the per-session pads bought on the Day 1 $106 consumables row, about $6 inside the $106) on the door table next to the scanner. Stage one spare dark felt-tip marker at the door table as the door-table marker, bought on the Day 1 consumables row as the fifth marker (about $1 inside the row's $106; the other four ride the equipment shelf's Day 1, Day 4, and Day 8 pull-and-return chains), and one half-ream box of blank paper as the paper stock box (about $3 inside the $90 snacks-and-prints operating line), both staged at the door table beside the scanner: the midday authority-switch tent card and the knock-note both pull from here, so a solo instructor never hunts for a writing tool mid-lesson. Both stay at the door table all session, riding neither a day-box nor the field bag. Set one pump bottle of sunscreen on the door table beside the scanner too, the self-apply bottle the heat-illness bullet names for the 9:15 walk-out count; it stays at the door table all session like the marker and the paper. Pull the combination-lock door-table lockbox out of the Day 10 box (the gallery strike packed it there) and set it on the equipment shelf, then set its combination there, a code distinct from the med lockbox and the medication cooler bag, held by the instructor only; pull the 12 phone pouches out of the lockbox (the Day 10 close beat staged them there at the final dismissal), then re-label them for the new session: peel last session's painter's-tape name strips off the pouches and trash them, so no prior session's first names linger; tear 12 fresh strips from the Day 8 painter's tape roll on the equipment shelf; write the new session's 12 camper first names off the Airtable roster, one name per strip, with the door-table marker; and stick one strip on each pouch. The name strips the pouches carry are fresh for this session's roster, so the Day 1 check-in's drop and the 11:15 pickup's hand-back both name the right camper. Then carry the lockbox to the door table and stage the 12 name-labeled resealable phone pouches inside it there. The lockbox sits on the door table all session and rides neither a day-box nor the field bag. Lock the ten day-boxes in the storage closet; the key lives with the instructor only, and the section 08 move-out close returns the key to the venue office after the emptied closet is relocked, so no key rides between sessions.

The mid-session restock, 30 minutes, Wednesday evening after Day 3 (June 16): reprint anything the Day 4 and Day 5 boxes came up short on (deploy log sheets, graph charts, failure log sheets, before-and-after portfolio pages), recharge the Day 4 and 5 gear, check the Tue-Thu AI-design print schedule is on track and clear any failed print, re-queueing it from the saved file, and check the filament: if either printer's spool reads under about one-quarter, swap in the mid-week spare from the equipment shelf, since the six fixed revisions print Friday afternoon. Top up the sick kit's working stock (glove pairs, absorbent pads, emesis bags, disinfectant wipes, zip bags, thermometer probe covers) from the sealed refill pack beside the first-aid kit, replacing whatever the week's episodes consumed, so the second half of the session runs on a full tray. Check the venue printer's toner gauge before the restock reprints: if it reads under about one-quarter and the camp's spare cartridge is still sealed in the Day 9 box, swap it in and hand the spent cartridge to venue staff for recycling, and order a fresh spare on the next session's consumables cart. Nothing restocks itself and nothing is bought retail mid-week: the $1,263/session materials line buys the consumables below as one cart, ordered a month before, quote-capped at $1,263: the ceiling is the $286 day rows plus the $977 reserve; whatever the one-cart total comes in under it is released, never re-budgeted; if the cart exceeds the ceiling the founder decides in the open at order time, scope cut or contingency draw, never a silent shortfall.

07 · Budget sketch

Honest math for one solo-instructor session.

12 campers × $425 tuition, one two-week session (ten one-hour lessons). Equipment is a one-time startup cost (amortized over 3 summers); the operating table shows a single steady-state session. A donor-funded scholarship bench covers 2 of 12 seats. (The year-1 launch costs, entity, ads, compliance stack, are itemized separately in §10's launch ledger, so these two budgets never double-count.)

The session runs $3,270 in the red at $425 tuition, because the venue bills actual room hours (about 34.3 hours at $75/hr, $2,575: the ~25.8 session hours (8:45 prep through 11:15 pickup daily, 11:45 dismissal plus ~20-min gallery strike on Day 10), the 4-hour Session Zero kitting Saturday, which needs venue access because the day-boxes print and pack on site, the 30-minute Wednesday-evening restock after Day 3 (June 16), the 3-hour Friday-afternoon print-tending block after Day 5 (June 18), which the fixed-revision prints need the room for, and the ~1-hour post-session equipment move-out after the strike), not the ten teaching hours the old line assumed. Two $2.5k founding sponsorships cover that shortfall, the scholarship bench (2 seats/session), and an equipment-refresh reserve. The $425 price point holds because that is what makes the cohort accessible; the sponsors underwrite the margin by design. Year 2 adds a second session at the same venue, spreading startup costs across twenty lessons instead of ten.

09 · Success metrics

We measure the skill, not the vibe.

Camper growth
  • Pre/post assessment: verify-or-trust a set of AI claims, target +40% accuracy on "checked it and here's the evidence"
  • 100% of campers ship a capstone with a completed credit roll
  • Rubric-scored judgment: taste-panel scores align with instructor panel by Day 8
Family verdict
  • Parent NPS (Net Promoter Score, -100 to +100) ≥ 60 at Showcase exit survey
  • ≥ 70% of families say camper "talks about checking AI output at home" (the dinner-table test)
  • ≥ 50% re-enroll or refer for Summer 2028
Program health
  • Enrollment: 12 campers, waitlist ≥ 6 by May 1
  • Safety: zero unsupervised tool incidents; one background-checked adult supervises all 12 campers every minute of every session; field missions move as a single group, no exceptions
  • Financial: sponsorship + scholarship bench fully funded before session 1

10 · Execution plan

The launch plan: automation for the paperwork, humans for the judgment.

This camp can be built by one operator + a stack of real APIs, with humans kept exactly where the law, insurers, and child safety require them: supervising children and owning judgment calls. Below: the full launch plan, seven phases, T-minus timeline, itemized budget, kill gates, and the honest list of steps that cannot be human-free. Every named API was verified to exist in Aug 2026; every marketplace that doesn't expose an API is flagged and given a workaround.

The operating thesis APIs do the paperwork: form the entity, bind insurance, run background checks, push ads, collect tuition, text parents, track rosters. Humans own the judgment: permit walk-throughs, insurance riders, adjudicating a flagged background check, and, non-negotiably, supervising children. Roughly 90% of the launch tasks run without a human touching them; the remaining 10% is the part that makes it legal and safe, compressed into seven single-decision human gates.
Phase 0 · T-22 → T-20 weeks (Jan 2027)

Entity & money

~3 weeks · ~$3,200
  • Stripe Atlas, form the LLC (Delaware via Atlas), EIN auto-issued by the IRS within days, Mercury operating account through Atlas's bank partner. verified API
  • Honest note: Atlas defaults to Delaware; operating in California means foreign qualification ($70) + CA's $800/yr franchise tax anyway. That $870 is real and budgeted below, not a surprise.
  • DocuSign eSignature API, account + templates for the four paper shapes we need: the instructor's W-2 offer and employment agreement (contractor arrangements are off the table; the instructor is a W-2 employee on Gusto payroll), venue agreement, parent waiver, and the Day 6 guest media release (sent the week before the session; the signed copy files into the instructor folder before Session Zero). verified API Pricing honesty: API plans are quote-based; budget $1.8–4k/yr. Decision rule, T-22w: the quote is in hand before Entity + bank close. If the quote exceeds $1,800, the SignWell-class API fallback executes at about $600/yr instead, and the $1,800 launch-ledger line buys the fallback with the difference released, never a shortfall. The $1,800 is a ceiling, not a low-end wish. (Checked this run: SignWell API pricing is pay-as-you-go at $0.85 per document after 25 free documents a month, and the camp sends roughly 20 documents a year, so the ~$600 fallback figure is conservative.)
Kill gate 0, Entity + bank not live in 3 weeks → stop. Nothing downstream can hold money or sign paper.
Phase 1 · T-20 → T-16 weeks (Jan–Feb)

Compliance & insurance

~4 weeks · ~$3,450

Regulatory reality first (California, 2026): a seasonal, primarily-recreational summer day camp is exempt from child-care facility licensing (Health and Safety Code §1596.792, with CDSS, the California Department of Social Services, status confirmed in writing at T-20), but that exemption walks you into two other regimes: (a) the Organized Camps law (HSC §18897 et seq. + Title 17 CCR §§30700-30741) with a permit from the county health department and a qualified on-site Health Supervisor; and (b) AB 506, which requires background checks, mandated-reporter training, and a child-abuse-prevention policy from youth-service organizations, we apply it in full regardless of the for-profit edge case. This plan complies with all three. human seam: county inspector

  • Thimble API (thimble.com/api), binds base General Liability by API, by the job, month, or year, and issues the certificate of insurance naming the venue host as additional insured, which is what actually unblocks the venue booking. verified API Pricing honesty: Thimble publishes a national average of about $42/mo (about $504/yr) with policies starting at $17/mo, and independent reviews put the real-world blended average near $94/mo (about $1,128/yr); the camp class serving ages 10-14 in California, with hand tools and walking field missions, prices above the national small-business average. Bind rule, T-20w: the annual quote is in hand before the venue deposit; if the quote exceeds $1,700, the broker who placed the $1,200 abuse/molestation rider rebids the GL as a package and the $1,700 launch-ledger line still binds the GL alone, never a shortfall; any difference under $1,700 is released, never re-budgeted. The $1,700 is a ceiling, not a quote.
  • Honest seam: the abuse & molestation endorsement, which county inspectors and sane parents require, is underwritten by specialists (camp insurers like K&K), not purchasable via any self-serve API. One broker call. Pricing honesty: K&K's published 2026 youth day camp program prices the sexual misconduct liability option (Option 1, $250K per insured event / $1M aggregate, defense within limits) at $0.45 per camper per week with a $150 minimum premium, which would put a 12-camper, 2-week session at the $150 minimum, but that option is not sold stand-alone: it requires K&K's own GL program, which this plan does not use (the GL binds through Thimble by API), so the published floor is an anchor, not a buy. The cheaper published Option 2 ($100 flat, reimbursement of defense costs only) is not liability coverage and does not satisfy a county inspector. Bind rule, T-20w: the broker's annual quote is in hand before the venue deposit; $1,200 is the quote-capped ceiling, and about $1,200 inside the $1,200 is the annual endorsement alone; if the quote exceeds $1,200 the broker re-shops with competing camp insurers (the run-896 GL package rebid already runs through this same broker); because the endorsement is county-required it cannot be dropped or cut to the defense-only option, so a sustained overage above the ceiling is a founder launch decision at T-20w, in the open, never a silent shortfall. Any difference under $1,200 is released, never re-budgeted.
  • Checkr API, invite + run 1 adult background check (the instructor) at ~$65 incl. county fees. verified API Pricing honesty: Checkr publishes the Basic package at $29.99 per report, pay-as-you-go with no contract, plus court and database fees passed through at cost. Order rule, T-20w: the founder orders the single instructor report before the T-16 hiring sprint; San Mateo County pass-through fees ride inside the $65; $65 is a ceiling, not a quote, and whatever the county fees come in under is released, never re-budgeted. FCRA adverse-action review is the human adjudication seam: a flagged report never auto-clears, and a check not clean by T-10 fires kill gate 3, the session postpones, non-negotiable.
  • AB 506 / mandated-reporter training, online. Pricing honesty: California's own mandated-reporter training, run by CDSS with the Office of Child Abuse Prevention, is free 24/7 self-paced in English and Spanish with a CDSS-issued completion certificate, and AB 506 explicitly allows organizations to use it. Paid third-party AB 506 courses run about $15-25 per seat; the free path trades paid tracking for manual recordkeeping, which the compliance folder already does. Completion rule, T-16: the instructor's certificate is filed before the session is announced; a certificate not on file by T-10 fires kill gate 3 alongside the background check, the session postpones, non-negotiable. About $20 inside the $20 is one paid seat if the founder chooses it; the free CDSS path releases the $20, never re-budgeted. The $20 is a ceiling, not a spend.
  • County organized-camp permit, filed at T-20. Pricing honesty: San Mateo County EHS publishes no flat organized-camp permit fee; it bills fee-for-service at its fully burdened hourly rate, $311/hr effective Jan 1, 2026 (Board File 24-990), and the published California-county analog, Santa Barbara County EHS's 2026 camp plan-check form, bills a nonrefundable $149 application plus $220/hr plan review and inspection. A clean 12-camper day camp with no food, pool, or water costs the application plus under an hour of review and the one site walk-through, so $400 is a defensible ceiling. Filing rule, T-20: the founder files the application online and asks the specialist for the time estimate; if the estimate exceeds $400 the decision lands before the venue deposit, and an application not accepted by T-16 fires kill gate 1 regardless. The permit is annual, so one bind covers both June sessions and the §07 insurance row's about-$200 share is the same annual, not a second buy; whatever the county bills under $400 is released, never re-budgeted.
Kill gate 1, No insurance binder + permit application accepted by T-16 → stop before the venue deposit moves (nothing is refundable-proof at that point). The county can simply be slow; that's a stop, not a workaround.
Phase 2 · T-20 → T-14 weeks (Feb–Mar)

Venue

~4 weeks (overlaps P1) · deposit $300
  • Requirements spec, written once and reused: 1,500+ sq ft makerspace, quiet interview room, secure outdoor access, walkable block, gallery wall, room screen or projector, on-site laser printer, reliable wi-fi sized for 8+ laptops with verifiable content filtering, single-use restroom adjacent to the main room (door visible from the instructor's seat), lockable on-site storage for the day-boxes and equipment June 12–25, weekday 8am–6pm access June 7–25 plus one Saturday 4-hour kitting block (June 12, 8am–12pm) plus one 30-minute Wednesday-evening restock block after Day 3 (June 16) plus one 3-hour Friday-afternoon print-tending block after Day 5 (June 18, the fixed-revision print window), COI naming the host.
  • Peerspace / Tagvenue, flagged honestly: neither exposes a public booking or inquiry API (verified Aug 2026; they are message-and-book marketplaces). no public API
  • Workaround: scripted marketplace search + browser automation builds a shortlist of 6 candidate venues with pricing and availability into Airtable; the operator makes one decision, pick + approve deposit (card on file). Hosts reply in-marketplace; the final booking is deliberately not scripted.
  • Budget anchor: ~$2,575/session (about 34.3 hours of room time at the ~$75/h makerspace rate, quote-capped at $75/hr, see the Phase 2 venue-rate rule: the $75/hr is anchored to the San Mateo County Community College District's published July 2026 facilities fee schedule, for-profit Classroom 50 and under at $75/hr (nonprofit $50/hr), corroborated by UW Bothell's 2026 classroom rates (small classrooms up to 30 at $50/hr, big classrooms 31-60 at $75/hr); dedicated makerspace event rooms and Peerspace listings price higher, about $150-$375/hr, so the plan's rate assumes a classroom-style rental (school, church, or community-college room) with the camp's own equipment, not a turnkey makerspace; a signed quote above $75/hr draws first on the $900 contingency share, and a quote the contingency cannot cover fires kill gate 2's die terms, not a second venue buy: the ~25.8 session hours (8:45 prep through 11:15 pickup daily, 11:45 dismissal plus ~20-min gallery strike on Day 10), the 4-hour Session Zero kitting Saturday, plus the 30-minute mid-week restock after Day 3 (June 16), plus the 3-hour Friday-afternoon print-tending block after Day 5 (June 18, the fixed-revision print window), plus the ~1-hour equipment move-out after the Day 10 gallery strike (June 25)), deposit due at booking.
  • Venue agreement carries the break-glass cancellation-notice clause: the DocuSign venue agreement (signed by T-14 under kill gate 2) includes a clause authorizing the camp's designated break-glass adult, as named on the camp's keyholder roster at the time of notice, to send written notice cancelling or releasing the remaining dates on the camp's behalf; the notice must quote the clause and the roster entry, so the authority is on the contract, not on the keyholder's word alone. The clause also pins the notice's timing: the release notice is effective upon sending by the agreement's named notice method, not upon the venue's receipt, so on the night the clause matters, when the legal-notice address reaches the venue's legal entity but no person answers, the release is timed by the keyholder's sent notice, and the venue cannot later claim the cancellation was late or that remaining-date fees are owed. The clause also pins the break-glass notice's email sufficiency: at T-14 signing the founder reads the agreement's notice provision and the clause adopts its email path when one is named; if the venue's standard form names only certified mail, the break-glass clause adds email as a permitted method for this notice type only, so the keyholder at 9 PM sends the release by email from a phone and the effective-upon-sending timing attaches to the sent email, not to a certified-mail drop no one can reach after hours. The clause also pins the break-glass notice's sender identity to the roster name, not the sending domain: the keyholder at 9 PM sends from a personal phone with a personal sending address, so the notice's identity is the quoted roster entry, not the email domain, and the venue verifies the sender by the roster name it already holds, the name put in writing at signing, at the T-6w build, and with every keyholder change, so a personal sending address cannot dispute that the notice came from the camp's authorized sender. The clause also pins the break-glass notice's subject-line convention: the 9 PM email's subject line names the clause and quotes the remaining session dates, so the release is triage-visible in the venue's inbox on the night it goes out, not a clause-quoting body under a generic subject. The convention's dates are read off a printed page, never computed at 9 PM: the sealed break-glass envelope the T-6w build seals holds a one-page session calendar listing the ten teaching dates with their calendar dates, so the keyholder circles the dates printed after the broadcast night and pastes them into the subject line. The convention's clause name is never typed at 9 PM either: the sealed break-glass envelope holds a subject-line template beside the calendar, a printed page with the break-glass cancellation-notice clause's name already printed and a blank date line to fill, so the keyholder copies the circled dates onto the template's date line and reads the clause name off the template verbatim, typing no fixed text on the worst evening of the session, and a mistyped clause name can never undercut the triage visibility the convention exists for. The notice's quoted body is never typed at 9 PM either: the sealed break-glass envelope holds a printed clause-quote card and a printed roster card beside the calendar and the template, the clause-quote card carrying the break-glass cancellation-notice clause's full text printed from the signed agreement, with the clause's operative authority passage, the sentence granting the designated break-glass adult authority to send written notice cancelling or releasing the remaining dates, re-printed in an isolated box at the top of the card, the passage alone in larger type, the box assembled at print time by copying the passage verbatim from the card's own full-text print, never re-typed from memory, and read back against the signed agreement before the envelope is sealed, and the roster card carrying the keyholder's roster entry as the venue holds it, so the keyholder copies the boxed operative passage out of the isolated box and the roster entry into the email body verbatim, never starting from an adjacent unmarked line of the full text, and the authority the venue reads is the contract's own words, not the keyholder's memory of them, not the keyholder's choice of fragment, and not a box the founder re-typed. The roster card is re-printed in the re-walk sitting whenever the keyholder changes, so a 9 PM body can never quote a stale name; the clause-quote card is not re-printed on a keyholder change, because the clause did not change, so the re-sealed envelope holds the new roster card beside the untouched boxed card; a date shift moves neither the clause nor the roster, so the cards ride the date-shift re-print with their contents and their box unchanged, the date-shift re-seal printing a fresh envelope ID across the new band and retiring the old one, so the Day 1 photo read always covers the current envelope. If the session dates ever shift after signing, the founder re-prints and re-seals the envelope the same day the dates move, so no 9 PM trigger can fire on a stale calendar, and the template rides the re-print beside the calendar. The clause authorizes by role, not by name: the agreement is signed eight weeks before the T-6w build names the keyholder, so the roster always carries the current keyholder's name, and the venue's designated contact, the agreement's signing counterparty, and the agreement's legal-notice address are recorded on the roster at signing, the counterparty as the standing escalation fallback if the contact goes silent and the legal-notice address as the third line that cannot turn over with staff, read off the agreement's own notice provision at signing; the contact line is re-confirmed at the T-2w step the Phase 6 week-before window names; if no keyholder is named at signing, the founder sends the venue the roster name the week the keyholder is named, no later than the T-6w build, and whenever the keyholder changes afterward the founder sends the venue the updated roster name in writing as part of the re-walk the T-6w row requires, so the name the venue holds never lags the person who might send the notice.
Kill gate 2, No signed venue by T-14 → no June session. The venue is the long pole; there is no second choice without moving the cohort's dates.
Phase 3 · T-16 → T-10 weeks (Feb–early Apr)

Staffing: one instructor

~6 weeks (overlaps P2) · ~$300 sourcing + $2,000/session comp
  • AB5 settled, not dodged: the instructor is either the founder operating the camp (no classification question at all) or a W-2 employee on Gusto payroll (~$55/mo + ~$255 employer-side taxes per session at published rates), with California workers' comp bound before Day 1. Under the ABC test (AB5, Labor Code §2775) an on-site, on-schedule instructor delivering the camp's core service is an employee, so contractor arrangements, and the Deel contractor flow the original plan named, are off the table by design. Pricing honesty: Gusto publishes the Simple plan at $49/mo plus $6 per person (the base rose from $40 to $49 in March 2026); one W-2 employee costs $55/mo, so three months is about $165, not the $120 the old $40 figure implied. Employer-side taxes on $2,000 of session wages run about $235 at published rates (Social Security 6.2%, Medicare 1.45%, FUTA 0.6% on the first $7,000 with California's credit-reduction risk, CA SUI 3.4% new-employer rate on the first $7,000 per CA EDD, CA ETT 0.1%; SDI is employee-side and not an employer cost); the $255 is a ceiling, not a computed quote. Activation rule, T-16: the Gusto account opens only when a non-founder W-2 instructor signs the offer in Phase 3; if the founder operates the camp, the account never opens and the whole $420 releases, never re-budgeted; the $420 is a ceiling, not a quote, and whatever the subscription plus taxes come in under it is released, never re-budgeted. Pricing honesty: the WCIRB reports the average California charged rate at $1.64 per $100 of payroll for the first half of 2026 (WorkCompCentral, Oct 9, 2026), and the insurance commissioner approved a 6.6% advisory pure premium increase effective Sept 1, 2026, so the computed premium on $2,000 of session wages is only about $20-$35; the $450 ceiling covers the one-employee policy minimum premium plus policy and broker fees, not the computed rate. Bind rule, T-16: the workers' comp policy binds only when a non-founder W-2 instructor signs the offer in Phase 3; if the founder operates the camp, the policy is $0 and the whole $450 releases, never re-budgeted; $450 is a ceiling, not a quote, and whatever the broker binds under it is released, never re-budgeted; the policy binds before Day 1. Verify with employment counsel before launch.
  • Sourcing: one hire through local maker-space and school job boards (~$300 in listings). Upwork is flagged honestly, its hiring API is restricted (enterprise/managed access, not open for automated posting), so it is a backup, not the plan. restricted API Pricing honesty: Craigslist charges $75 per 30-day job posting in the SF Bay Area, the only US metro at the $75 premium; the maker-space and school job boards named above post free as community listings, so the $300 ceiling covers up to four Craigslist postings alongside the free boards. Posting rule, T-16: the founder posts the listings at the start of Phase 3; each posting runs 30 days; $300 is a ceiling, not a quote, and whatever the postings cost under it is released, never re-budgeted; under the founder-as-instructor path the listings never post and the whole $300 releases, never re-budgeted, mirroring the Gusto activation rule; no instructor signed with a clean background check by T-10 still fires kill gate 3.
  • Screening: async video interview transcribed by a speech-to-text API and scored against a published rubric (kid-safety judgment ranked above technical skill); two reference calls scheduled by Twilio; decision recorded in Airtable.
  • Adjudication seam: a flagged background check goes to a human decision (FCRA, the Fair Credit Reporting Act, adverse-action review). No auto-reject, ever.
  • Structure: 1 instructor behind the 1:12 cap. The adult-in-the-room floor is the irreducible human core of this plan, see Honest Seams below. There is no degraded staffing mode: the format is built so one adult is sufficient, and anything that needs a second adult does not ship.
Kill gate 3, No instructor with a clean background check by T-10 → postpone. There is exactly one adult in the room; there is no smaller crew to fall back to.
Phase 4 · T-18 → T-4 weeks (Feb–mid May)

Camper acquisition

~14 weeks · ~$2,800
  • Meta Marketing API + Google Ads API, both real, both scriptable: launch, budget, pause, and report by code. verified APIs $2,500 spend plan; target CPL (cost per lead) $40–70, implied CAC (customer acquisition cost) ≈ $210/camper. Pricing honesty: WordStream's 2026 Google Ads benchmarks put Education and Instruction CPL at $77.48 (PPC Chief's consolidated 2026 set: $90.02), so the plan's $40-$70 target is the optimistic bound and the funnel's 45-lead figure holds only at or below benchmark CPL. The $2,500 is a spend ceiling, not a forecast: the ad accounts launch with $2,500 API-side budget caps, whatever comes in under it is released, never re-budgeted, and the CPL over $90 two-week kill switch in the next bullet is the binding guard, it pauses the spend automatically.
  • Funnel math (honest version): ~$2.5k spend → ~45 qualified leads → 12 enrollments at ~27% lead→paid conversion. If CPL runs > $90 for two straight weeks, ad sets pause automatically, the API kills its own spend.
  • Stripe Payment Links (created via API), $425 tuition, deposit option, scholarship codes. verified API Processing 2.9% + 30¢ ≈ $152/session, booked on the §07 operating table's payment-processing row.
  • Typeform API intake (camper info, allergies, pickup authorizations, accommodation requests) webhooked into Airtable; DocuSign API sends the liability waiver + photo release automatically on payment. verified APIs Pricing honesty (October 2026): Typeform published cards price Basic at $28/mo billed yearly and $39/mo month-to-month (100 responses per month, 1 user); the paid plans bill yearly-only, so a 3-month launch subscription is only buyable month-to-month, about $117 for the window. File upload is a paid-plan feature with a 1GB limit on Basic, plenty for the parent-provided allergy-plan PDFs, so Plus is not needed. The free plan's 10 responses per month cannot carry a 12-camper intake with a waitlist, so the plan is paid month-to-month Basic with no annual lock. Subscription rule: the subscription opens when the enrollment forms go live at the start of Phase 4 and cancels the month after session 1 fills, or at T-4, whichever comes first; $150 is a ceiling, not a quote, and whatever the three monthly billings come in under it is released, never re-budgeted.
  • Landing page: this site, enrollment CTAs activate when the live Payment Link publishes at T-18. Hosting is free (GitHub Pages); forms and payments are all API-side.
Kill gate 4 (soft, T-8), fewer than 6 paid → cut ad spend to $800 retarget-only. Hard, T-4: fewer than 10 paid → cancel session, refund in full via Stripe, run the wind-down checklist (the seven-step version the instructor-sick-day bullet enumerates: the T-6w build already scheduled all ten crisis broadcasts, so step one is disarming them and step six edits the greeting's TTS text). Binding re-score gate: if the post-pilot panel re-score has not published on this page by Friday, May 14, 2027, or clears below 9.0, the session cancels on the same terms, enrollments or not: 9.0 or the camp does not run. Cancelling at T-4 strands ≈ $4.7k (sunk ad spend + the pilot spend + non-refundable setup + "the first AI-seat billing cycle, about $300" itemized: the T-6w build provisions the 12 seats before the T-4 gate, and on month-to-month business billing the first cycle bills at purchase and cancel stops future renewals only, OpenAI's published seat policy keeps the current month billed on any reduction, so the first of the 2 billed months is spent whether the session runs or not), that number is the plan's true worst case, and it's why the gates exist. Why ten: ten paid seats plus the two donor-funded scholarship seats equal the full 12-seat cohort, 12 x $425 = $5,100 against the $8,370 per-session operating budget (itemized in §07). A full session already runs $3,270 in the red, which the founding sponsorships absorb by design; at nine paid seats plus the two donor-funded scholarship seats, eleven revenue-generating seats, the hole is about $3,695 (11 x $425 = $4,675 against $8,370), and that gap would come out of the equipment-refresh reserve, so it cancels at the gate instead of burning the reserve.

Honest seams, the humans this plan refuses to remove

Each seam is compressed to a single human decision, made once (or once a day), with everything else prepared by the stack:

  • 1 · County health inspector, the organized-camp permit requires a human walk-through and sign-off at the venue. One meeting, T-2 weeks.
  • 2 · Insurance broker, the abuse & molestation endorsement isn't self-serve on any API. One call, T-20 weeks.
  • 3 · Background-check adjudication, FCRA adverse-action review of any flagged candidate. A human reads, a human decides, per candidate.
  • 4 · Venue deposit approval, one decision on a shortlist of six. Money moves only after the click.
  • 5 · The adult in the room, one trained, background-checked, first-aid-certified adult on site every single minute campers are present, backed by the automated admin stack (Airtable, Twilio, Typeform). The 1:12 cap is a hard ceiling, and the 60-minute lesson format with self-directed project blocks is what makes one adult sufficient. This isn't overhead; it's the product.
  • 6 · Medication & incident command, the instructor administers meds and owns every incident call. Never automatable, never delegated to software.
  • 7 · Pickup authorization, photo-ID match against the signed authorization record, at the door, every day. The robot never dismisses a child.

Correction for the record: an earlier draft cited "AB-2621" as the CA camp-licensing bill. Verified against leginfo, AB 2621 is not camp legislation (it's regional climate-planning in 2020, unemployment-insurance in 2022). The real anchors are HSC §1596.792 (child-care exemption), HSC §18897 et seq. + Title 17 CCR §§30700-30741 (organized camps), and AB 506 (youth-org background checks + mandated-reporter training). This page keeps the receipts.

11 · The red team

We grade ourselves harder than any parent will.

This camp teaches kids to check AI's work. The least we can do is check our own. Before a single parent sees this plan, a seven-person panel red-teams it against one question: could one instructor plausibly teach this camp with one hour of direct instruction a day? The panel's scores and its demands are published here, including the ones we have not cleared yet. Re-scored 2026-09-07 after the device-free take-home option and the pilot evidence plan were published: 8.3/10. The plan ships no session until the panel clears 9.0.

The instructor · 8.5/10

"Teachable. The handouts exist."

The run-of-show plans, the 30-minute prep lists, and now the ten printed handouts are real lesson plans. The project block states plainly that the instructor stays in the room, silent, supervising. The remaining points are a pilot session: no paper plan, however complete, finds every surprise a real ten-year-old will invent.

The parent · 8.5/10

"The take-home question is answered."

The day is pinned to clock times (9:15 drop-off, 11:15 pickup), the project block's supervision is stated in plain language, and every project block runs on printed sheets with no device assumed. The device-free take-home option is now stated outright: paper paths for everything, no shared device goes home, conversation cards for the dinner table. Still open: the first real parent walkthrough night of the safety plan, scheduled for the week of the April 2027 pilot.

The 11-year-old camper · 8.5/10

"The days sound fun. Don't leave me stuck."

The handouts give the quiet 45 minutes a real structure: numbered steps, minute marks, a named job for finishing early, and a stuck protocol. A ten-year-old with no adult teaching can follow a printed page. The remaining points belong to a real ten-year-old in the room; paper cannot spend them.

The 14-year-old camper · 8/10

"Not babyish. Keep the hard versions real."

The senior extensions now sit inside the handouts themselves, not just the lesson plans: computing forecast error, writing the "what we almost let through" case study, sketching the rover waypoint plan. The core pace still skews young on paper; a pilot will tell whether the hard versions are hard enough. Flagged and fixed since the re-score: the pilot recruited ages 10 to 12 only, so the senior extensions had no testers and this card's open question could not be answered on pilot day. The cohort is now four 10-12s and four 13-14s, and the pilot's exit interview asks the 13-14s directly whether the hard versions were hard enough. Scores untouched; the points still belong to a real pilot day.

The safety officer · 8/10

"One adult works, if no minute goes unwatched."

Both earlier demands are cleared: continuous instructor presence through the project block, and the instructor named as the on-site Health Supervisor for the county organized-camp permit. No new findings this round; the remaining points belong to a real county inspector's walk-through, which no website can score.

The budget realist · 8/10

"The math checks. The margin is thin, and it says so."

Per-session and launch arithmetic reconcile. Flagged: the Twilio ping times were left over from a full-day format (fixed to the 9:15/11:15 day), and instructor pay is now stated against all present hours, not just teaching hours. Flagged and fixed since the re-score: the venue line still billed ten one-hour lessons; it now bills the actual room time, about 34.3 hours at $75, so the session's net is -$3,270 per session, stated outright as sponsor-underwritten, and gate 4's cancel math matches it (the earlier $575 figure was an intermediate step, superseded when the move-out hour and the full room-time accounting landed).

Flagged and fixed in this pass: the plan ended the physical world at the Day 10 gallery strike, with venue access and lockable storage running through June 25, but named no equipment move-out: the ten day-boxes, the laptop cart, the 24-port charging tray, the rover-course kit, the field bag, and the door-table scanner all had to leave the venue with no named owner, no hour, and no line. The §08 venue bullet now names the move-out, about one hour after the gallery strike on June 25, as founder operator labor outside the instructor's paid hours (a hired W-2 instructor does no unpaid overtime under California wage law), and the §07 venue line bills the actual room hour at $75: 34.3 hours, $2,575 per session, operating total $8,370, per-session net -$3,270, gate-4 eleven-seat math updated to an about-$3,695 hole (11 x $425 = $4,675 against $8,370), and the year-1 cash reconciliation updated to about $18.2k net. Two $2.5k founding sponsorships still cover the shortfall, the two scholarship seats, and the equipment-refresh reserve: $3,270 plus 2 x $425 = $4,120 against $5,000. Scores untouched.

The curriculum designer · 8.5/10

"The evidence plan is named. Now run it."

Minute-by-minute run-of-shows with junior/senior splits, plus ten printed handouts with stuck protocols and no laptop assumption. The field-test demand is now a stated evidence plan in §04: a pilot day on April 17, 2027 with eight volunteer campers (four 10-12s, four 13-14s), five measured numbers, a published success bar, and a re-score on this page after the pilot. Panel verdict

8.3/10. Below the 9.0 bar. Not launched.

What the panel demanded, and what changed on this page: the full handout kit is now published in §03b, all ten project-block sheets written in full; the day is pinned to clock times (9:15 drop-off, 11:15 pickup, Day 10 to 11:45 with the parents' showcase at 11:15-11:45) in §04; the instructor stays in the room through the project block, silent, supervising; the Health Supervisor role is named in the safety plan; parent pings match the day; pay is stated against all present hours; the device-free take-home option is stated outright in the FAQ; and the pilot evidence plan is published in §04, with a date (April 17, 2027), a recruiting channel, a published success bar, and a binding re-score on this page. The T-minus timeline in §10 now schedules the pilot, the walkthrough, and the binding re-score, and the hard kill gate at T-4 cannot clear until the re-score clears 9.0, so the 9.0 precondition is wired into the launch plan, not just stated here. What remains is all real-world: the pilot itself, the parent walkthrough night, the 14-year-old's question about whether the hard versions are hard enough, and the county inspector's walk-through, and the first session's real books against the budget lines. Those points belong to real people and a real day, not to better copywriting. 9.0 or the camp does not run.

12 · FAQ

The questions parents actually ask.

Does my kid need AI or coding experience?

None. We assume zero on Day 1 and teach every tool from the button up. The camp's core skills, observing, checking, building, asking, deciding, need no prerequisites. Kids who already code get harder variants of every mission.

Wait, is this two weeks of screens?

The opposite. Roughly half of every day is outside or at a workbench: walking the block with a camera, soldering a sensor, testing prints, driving rovers through an obstacle course. AI tools appear constantly, but as the thing being directed, checked, and out-performed, not the destination.

Soldering irons and 3D printers at age 10?

Every tool is introduced with a supervised demonstration, and no tool is ever used solo: heated or sharp tools run only at supervised stations with the instructor within arm's reach, with ventilation and PPE. The soldering iron is touched by the instructor only, while campers position parts and read the meter. With one adult and twelve campers, tool use is station-gated: only one heated station runs at a time, the rest of the group works on non-tool tasks. Our instructor owns tool safety personally.

Which AI tools do you use, and are they safe for kids?

School-managed accounts on mainstream, kid-safe AI tools (image generation, chat, CAD assistants) with content filtering on, no personal data entered, and strict "we don't feed it our faces or friends' names" rules taught on Day 2. Accounts are camp-owned and wiped at session end.

What does my kid actually take home?

A producer's portfolio: their verified dataset, the before-and-after portfolio page (their failed AI print photographed beside their human-fixed revision, with their own captions), sensor charts, the interview transcript (three hand-transcribed marker moments from the Moment Marker handout; the interview audio itself stays on the camp's recorders, which never leave the room), the debugging log, and the signed credit roll, plus a diploma reading Producer of AI Projects, Certified Human.

Is there a device-free option for take-home work?

Yes, and it is the default, not the exception. Every take-home item has a paper path: each day's project-block handout carries a perforated dinner-table conversation card as a tear-off strip (the ten questions are printed in the handout kit spec in §03b, one per day), the journal is a physical notebook, and anything that uploads to the camp gallery has a paper alternative (bring the journal in; at pickup the instructor runs the flagged pages through the flatbed scanner on the door table, about 30 seconds a page, and each scan lands in that camper's QR-linked gallery). Campers never take a shared device home; nothing that leaves the room needs a charger. Each day the camper tears off the conversation card at pickup, a single question for the dinner table, like "Ask a grown-up: when has a computer been confidently wrong in your job?" No screen, no app, no login required for any of it.

Is there financial aid?

Yes, a donor-funded scholarship bench covers 2 of 12 seats per session, prioritized through local school partners. Application is one short form; decisions are need-blind and made before enrollment closes.

My child has an IEP, ADHD, or sensory needs. Can they attend?

Very likely yes, and we tell you honestly before you pay. Enrollment asks about accommodations on the same form as allergies and pickup authorizations, and every family that names one gets a 15-minute call with us the week before camp to agree in writing on exactly what we will do: large-print handouts, seating with extra space, fidget tools and earplugs at your child's own seat, handout steps read aloud at the handoff, and field-mission routes checked for accessibility at our venue walk-through. What we cannot do with one instructor and twelve campers: provide 1:1 aides, run a separate quiet room, or change the line-of-sight supervision model. If we cannot support your child safely, you hear that before paying, and an enrolled family in that position gets a full refund.

What happens if my child feels sick at camp?

They never leave the instructor's sight. The sick camper rests in a chair beside the instructor's table while the rest of the group keeps working, the instructor takes a temperature, and a fever or any vomiting triggers same-day pickup: we message you over the camp number and your child rests until a listed adult arrives, expected within 30 minutes. A camper who vomited or ran a fever returns only after 24 hours symptom-free without medication, and you see that rule in the enrollment confirmation before you pay. If symptoms escalate, our incident tiers take over: first aid, then 911, then the parent call.

What happens if my child gets sick during a field walk?

The instructor stops the group on the route: everyone sits off the road in buddy pairs while your child sits with the instructor. An emesis bag and the thermometer come out of the field bag's first-aid kit right there, and a headache or nausea without fever gets water and about ten minutes seated, the group resuming if it passes. A fever or any vomiting means we message you over the camp number for same-day pickup, but the pickup is at the venue: the whole group walks straight back together along the mapped route, the instructor's count running aloud, and your child rests at the venue until you arrive. If your child cannot walk, the 911-first emergency chain fires immediately. The 24-hour symptom-free return rule applies on the walk as at the venue.

What happens if my child needs a midday medication during a field walk?

The dose is given on the route, not postponed to the venue: every route has a pre-mapped dose gate, a bench or shade point where the whole group sits together inside the instructor's sightline. Your child's buddy stands with them as the witness while the instructor gives the dose from the med lockbox or the lockable medication cooler bag, and the dose is logged with time and the instructor's initials beside the words exactly like every room dose. No one leaves the group, and the walk continues after the aloud count resumes.

What happens if my child's medication changes mid-session?

The change takes effect only on a fresh signed authorization form: no dose is ever given on a verbal instruction alone. Send the change over the camp number the evening before, sign the new form (DocuSign or paper at the door), and the instructor swaps the lockbox contents, updates the med/allergy sheet, and logs the change with time and the instructor's initials beside the words, all before the first dose under the new instruction. A discontinued medication comes home with you at pickup the same day, and a missed dose is logged with its reason, never guessed.

What if I need to reach camp after hours?

Send it to the camp number anyway. Nobody watches the line after the 11:15 pickup, but the instructor reads every message first thing each teaching morning and replies "got it" to each one, so anything you send overnight is handled before the doors open. A call after hours never rings the instructor's phone: it goes straight to the camp's voicemail greeting, which repeats the hours line, and the message is heard at the morning read. The hours line is printed in the footer of your pickup-authorization list. A true emergency after hours is a 911 call: the camp is closed and there is no night desk. Voicemail counts the same as a text: the instructor listens to every voicemail in the morning read. A voicemail never changes a medication or a pickup on its own: the signed form still has to land before anything changes, and a voicemail that disagrees with the signed form loses to the form.

If my child is taken to the hospital, who rides with them?

The paramedics transport your child; the instructor stays with the other eleven campers. One adult cannot leave the group unsupervised, and you agree to this configuration in the emergency-medical-treatment authorization you sign before paying. The 911 call comes first, then we call you, and you meet your child at the emergency department: your drive starts on the 911 call so you arrive with the ambulance. A one-page handoff sheet with your child's medication and allergy summary, what happened, and what was given rides with the paramedics, and we keep updating the camp number with the hospital name and address until a listed adult confirms they are on the way.

What happens if a thunderstorm rolls in during a field walk?

The mission aborts: thunder heard or lightning seen means the instructor calls the group together, counts aloud, and walks everyone straight back to the venue along the route you already see in the logistics pack, no sheltering under trees, no waiting it out in the open. The group does not step out again until 30 minutes after the last thunder. The day continues on the same indoor backup activities we pre-build for every weather day, so nothing is lost. You get a one-line message on the camp number when a mission comes in early, and the abort is logged.

What happens if the instructor is injured during a field walk?

The group freezes: the oldest camper says "Freeze, buddies" once, and everyone sits on the grass edge or the sidewalk, off the road, buddy pairs hold, and nobody leaves the route. The oldest camper pulls the instructor's phone from the field bag's named zip phone pocket and runs the locked-phone path, rehearsed at the Day 2 walk-out count: open the Control Center on an iPhone, or the quick-settings shade on an Android, from the lock screen with no passcode, tap Do Not Disturb on so no parent call can ring over the 911 call, then tap the Emergency call button and dial 911 with no passcode. The oldest camper reads the route card's printed 911 line to the dispatcher, the route street, the nearest cross street, and the mapped hard shelter, or the venue address off the pickup-list reverse on the venue-adjacent Day 2 safari; if the dispatcher asks what is wrong with the instructor, the oldest camper reads the instructor medical card from the same pocket, to the dispatcher only, never aloud to the group. When the 911 call ends, the oldest camper turns Do Not Disturb off by the same lock-screen path, no passcode needed, so the dispatcher's callback rings through, and answers the dispatcher first. No camper sends a parent message from the phone: the parent broadcast is pre-scheduled before the session and fires at 11:16 that day on its own if the instructor never cancels it, so parent comms arrive after the emergency response, in the same order the Tier 3 chain holds. The second oldest runs the aloud buddy count and keeps the group inside the instructor's sightline. The procedure is rehearsed with the campers at the Day 2 walk-out count and walked with parents at the parent walkthrough night, so every family knows it before paying. Like the room version, nobody touches the medication lockbox, the tools, the field kits, or the epinephrine.

It is hot but not hot enough to cancel the walk. How do you handle heat?

Sunscreen is self-applied at the door before the group leaves, and every camper carries a full water bottle with a spare bottle in the instructor's bag, so water is never the constraint. The instructor knows the signs: sweating through, headache, dizziness, or nausea means the camper sits in the shade with water for ten minutes while the group keeps working nearby, always in sight. If the camper is not back to normal after ten minutes, the walk ends early and the group comes back, with a message to you on the camp number. Anything more serious, confusion, slurred speech, or fainting, gets a 911 call first, like any emergency. Heat incidents are logged the same as every other safety incident.

What happens if my child gets separated from the group on a walk?

The group freezes on the spot: the instructor calls everyone together, sits them off the road in buddy pairs, and counts aloud. If your child is visible, the whole group walks together to close the gap, nobody runs ahead alone. If your child is not visible, the instructor calls 911 immediately from the phone in the field bag, reading the exact location off the route card, then calls you, the same 911-then-parent order as every emergency. One adult cannot leave eleven children to search, so nobody searches: the group stays together at the last point where your child was seen until the dispatcher or you say otherwise. The drill is rehearsed with the campers on the second walk of the session and walked with parents at the walkthrough night, so every family knows it before paying. Every incident is logged with a timestamp.

What happens if my child needs the restroom during a field walk?

The walk comes home. The mapped routes have no public restrooms, so before every walk the instructor sends everyone to the venue restroom first, and if your child needs one mid-walk they say so and the whole group walks straight back to the venue together; nobody is sent off alone and nobody ducks into a shop. Your child uses the venue restroom while the group counts back in, and the mission continues on the indoor backup plan. It is announced matter-of-factly at every walk-out, so asking is normal.

Why "producers" and not "prompt engineers"?

Prompting is a technique; producing is a job. A producer owns the outcome: the data, the checks, the fixes, and the blame when it's wrong. Prompting is one arrow in that quiver, we teach all ten.

What if AI gets better at all this by 2027?

Then the curriculum sharpens, the weakness list is re-audited each spring and days are rebuilt around whatever AI is currently worst at. The mission outlives any specific failure mode: the human who verifies, builds, and takes responsibility stays essential. (Also: we'll believe the demo when we can check it. That's the whole camp.)

Run 915 audit: organized-camp statute citation. Focus area: rubric item 6 (weakest, 8.3), regulatory-citation audit of the Organized Camps law anchor, after runs 887 through 914 closed every budget row and the day-of-week claims verified clean this run. GENUINE GAP FOUND AND FIXED. The plan cited the Organized Camps law as "HSC §30800 et seq. + Title 22 regs" in two places: the Phase 1 regulatory-reality paragraph and the "Correction for the record" note that claims "The real anchors are HSC §1596.792 (child-care exemption), HSC §30800 et seq. + Title 22 (organized camps), and AB 506" and "This page keeps the receipts." Verified against primary sources this run: the organized-camp statutes live at HSC §18897 et seq. (Division 13, Part 2.4, Camps), not §30800, per leginfo (SB 1087 amending §18897 to define "organized day camp"), lawserver (§18897.7, no organized camp operates without meeting the minimum standards), and Justia (2025 Code, HSC Division 13, Part 2.4, §18897.6); and the organized day camp regulations sit at Title 17 CCR §§30700-30741 (SB 1087 text: "Organized day camp sites shall be subject to the applicable requirements of Sections 30700 to 30741, inclusive, of Subchapter 6 of Title 17"), not Title 22, which is the CDSS child-care licensing title this camp is exempt from under §1596.792. The irony is recorded honestly: the "Correction for the record" note was itself correcting an earlier AB-2621 mis-citation, and carried the §30800 error forward while claiming the receipts were kept. A county inspector or a lawyer parent checking "HSC §30800" finds no organized-camp law there, which is exactly the credibility failure the safety-officer critic's 8/10 and the "human seam: county inspector" pill are sensitive to. The fix corrects both citations to "HSC §18897 et seq. + Title 17 CCR §§30700-30741" with no other prose changes; the §1596.792 exemption anchor and the AB 506 anchor were re-verified real and stand untouched. No budget-line changes: prose only, no new materials, no timing changes.
